fixes.explanation: A great famine, friend. The text says, “So there was a great famine in Samaria.” (2 Kings 6:25) Ben-hadad, king of Aram, had marched his whole army up to besiege the city. The siege went on so long that a donkey's head sold for eighty shekels of silver.

The text doesn't mention a plague. It says, “So there was a great famine in Samaria.” (2 Kings 6:25) The trouble was hunger, because Ben-hadad, king of Aram, besieged the city so long. A donkey's head sold for eighty shekels of silver.

No shaking ground in this one. The text says the city was besieged so long that there was a great famine (2 Kings 6:25). Ben-hadad, king of Aram, had marched up with his entire army. I think that was a hard stretch for the people of Samaria.

He tears his clothes. The text says, “When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes.” (2 Kings 6:30) As he passed by on the wall, the people saw the sackcloth under his clothes, right next to his skin. I think this part of the story hurts.

The text doesn't say he sends for her. It says he heard the woman's words and tore his clothes (2 Kings 6:30). As he passed by on the wall, the people saw the sackcloth underneath. This is a heavy moment, friend, and I think the king felt it.

No welcome mat at this house. Elisha, the prophet, tells the elders, “…when the messenger comes, shut the door to keep him out.” (2 Kings 6:32) He had just said the king sent someone to cut off his head. I think a shut door was the friendliest thing on offer.

It's the other way around. The king says, “This calamity is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?” (2 Kings 6:33) He is asking why he should keep waiting. I think that's a man running out of patience, friend.

Cheap and plentiful, friend! A seah of fine flour for one shekel, and two seahs of barley for one shekel (2 Kings 7:1). Compare that to a donkey's head at eighty shekels of silver. That's quite a drop, and Elisha says it's coming about this time tomorrow.

Not sell. Elisha says, “You will see it with your own eyes…” and then, “but you will not eat any of it.” (2 Kings 7:2) The officer had asked if the LORD making windows in heaven could really make this happen. He gets to watch it, and the eating is not for him.

Egypt never comes up in their plan. The four men say, “So come now, let us go over to the camp of the Arameans.” (2 Kings 7:4) They set out at twilight (2 Kings 7:5). Sometimes the answer is closer than you think.

That's it. The Lord had caused the Arameans to hear “…the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army…” (2 Kings 7:6) The Arameans said to one another that the king of Israel must have hired the kings of the Hittites and Egyptians to attack them. They took it from there.

Cracking walls? Not in this story, friend. The Lord had caused the Arameans to hear “…the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army…” (2 Kings 7:6) That sound alone had them running for their lives (2 Kings 7:7).

True. After hiding the first load, the text says they entered another tent, carried off some items from there, and hid them (2 Kings 7:8). They had gone into the first tent to eat and drink, and then carried off silver, gold and clothing. I think a person in that spot can lose track of how many trips they've made.

It's true, they went back for more. The text says that on returning, they entered another tent, carried off some items from there, and hid them (2 Kings 7:8). That's a second tent and a second load. I think the whole situation was a lot to take in.

That's what they say. “We are not doing what is right. Today is a day of good news.” (2 Kings 7:9) With their loot hidden, they stop and say it out loud to each other. They also say that if they wait until morning light, their sin will overtake them.

The king's household. They say, “Now, therefore, let us go and tell the king’s household.” (2 Kings 7:9) These are men who had been sitting at the entrance of the city gate. They call out to the gatekeepers, and the gatekeepers shout the news until it's reported to the king's household (2 Kings 7:10-11).

Still as high as before? Not a chance, friend. The text says a seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley sold for a shekel, “…according to the word of the LORD.” (2 Kings 7:16) Compare that to a donkey's head at eighty shekels of silver. The price Elisha, the prophet, announced is the price that came.

Doubling? Friend, the price went the other direction! The text says a seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley sold for a shekel, “…according to the word of the LORD.” (2 Kings 7:16) That's exactly what Elisha, the prophet, had said. The LORD's word did not miss by a single shekel.

That's not what the text says. The king had appointed him to be in charge of the gate, and the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died (2 Kings 7:17). That's what Elisha had foretold. It's a heavy part of the story.
